On the night Ramchandra Ray escaped, Sitaram was posted to stop Udayaditya from leaving. Though he refused to fight the prince he owed his life to, he asked Udayaditya to disarm and tie him up so he could claim he had been overpowered. When Udayaditya escaped, Sitaram instead took the initiative: he opened the prison door, carried him out under the pretext of a fire, and led him to safety.

Pratapaditya first planned to have two Pathan assassins kill Basanta Ray at the Simultali inn while he traveled to Jessore. That attempt failed when one Pathan’s brother diverted Basanta Ray’s retainers and the Pathan himself could not bring himself to kill him. Later, Pratapaditya ordered Basanta Ray’s death, and Abdul carried it out with a sword while Basanta Ray was praying.

In the inner quarters, Ramai is disguised as a middle-aged woman; Rammohan lifts and carries him off. Later, in the king’s room, Ramai appears openly as the jester; Rammohan grabs him by the scruff and throws him out.
Rukmini, living as Mangala, secretly prepared poison and sent it as medicine through Matangini; Surma took it and died before she could leave the palace.
By refusing the first escort, Vibha arrives too late: her husband has married another woman, leaving Vibha without a home in Chandradwip and shattering her hopes of happiness.

Rukmini manipulates Udayaditya into giving her his signet ring, which bears the Yubaraj’s name. Sitaram and Bhagavat use its seal on a forged petition accusing Pratapaditya of treason, making it appear Udayaditya is seeking the kingdom from the Emperor. Bhagavat presents the petition to Pratapaditya as proof of Udayaditya’s secret plot. Though Pratapaditya says he does not really believe the accusation, he uses it to justify imprisoning Udayaditya.

Udayaditya’s role in helping Ramchandra escape was a conspicuous defiance of Pratapaditya, who then began paying closer attention to his son. That scrutiny brought Udayaditya’s support for the dismissed guards to the king’s notice. When Surma secretly continued the aid, Pratapaditya ordered her sent to her father’s home, presenting it as a matter of state affairs.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s loneliness and grief for the loved ones who are gone, and his fear that nothing of his old life remains. He sings it first alone at sunset in Raigarh, reflecting on those he can no longer visit; later, in Jessore, he sings it while taking Vibha’s hand, confronted by the silent, empty rooms and the absence of the family who once gathered around him.

Rukmini discovered that Udayaditya was escaping with Basanta Ray and tried to alert the palace guards, but they ignored her warnings and failed to stop them. After Udayaditya reached Raigarh, Rukmini led Pratapaditya’s men to him. Pratapaditya ordered Udayaditya’s capture and Basanta Ray’s execution. When Udayaditya was seized, Basanta Ray was left without warning or protection; Muktiyar Khan’s soldiers entered the palace and killed him.

Pratapaditya gives Ramchandra a cool, minimal welcome: no fanfare, a delayed and small escort, and little attention when they meet. Later, Ramchandra’s court portrays Pratapaditya as beneath him—his courtiers mock his lineage and claim that marrying into Ramchandra’s family should redeem generations of his status.

Rukmini, three years older than Udayaditya, leaves Raigarh and lives outside Jessore under the name Mangala. She ingratiates herself with palace servants and, when the Rajmahishi seeks medicine to turn Udayaditya against Surma, prepares poison for Surma. As Surma is about to leave the palace, she takes the poison and dies.

Later, during a storm, Mangala enters Udayaditya’s chamber while he is grieving with a little girl. She reminds him of their past, claims he ruined her, and pleads for his love. He gives her his ring; she leaves, thinking her hold over him remains.

He first laments that royal birth has made him an heir to a burdensome throne rather than simply a son, and that his father’s scrutiny and neglect have left him convinced he cannot rule. Later, after the disasters he believes were caused by his weakness, he says he will leave the world. Brought before Pratapaditya, he admits he is unworthy of the kingdom and formally asks to be released from the throne. He swears before Ma-Kali never to claim any part of Jessore, sit on its throne, or touch its scepter, naming Samaraditya as heir, and asks to leave for Kashi.

Ramchandra sent the letter to Pratapaditya, but Nayanchand, afraid of what might happen if the king saw it, diverted it to the Mahishi. She kept it from both Pratapaditya and Vibha, then showed it to Basanta Ray. He misread Ramchandra’s angry declaration that he had renounced Vibha as a request to have her sent back to Chandradwip. He told the Mahishi to announce that version, so Vibha believed her husband had forgiven her and joyfully agreed to return.

Pratapaditya had the canal blocked with large sal-wood logs, expecting to stop Ramchandra’s boat. But Udayaditya’s party lowered Ramchandra from the palace roof into the boat by a makeshift rope, then hauled the boat over the logs. The guards couldn’t catch up: they lacked a ready gun, and the pursuing boat arrived too late.

Basanta Ray’s sitar is his cherished companion and outlet for joy, but as separation from Udayaditya overwhelms him, tears interrupt his playing until he cannot continue. He leaves the sitar behind, saying he will never play it again. Later, he describes it as still there but with broken strings that cannot be tuned—a reflection of his own sense that the happiness and closeness he once shared with his loved ones are gone. When he learns Udayaditya is imprisoned, his despair breaks through in his cry: “Dada, come to me!”

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for going out to involve himself in his subjects’ affairs and acting against his father’s wishes; he would stop officials from abusing them and help those in hardship. After Surma’s death, fear of Pratapaditya overcomes that resolve: he abandons plans to protect subjects, flees from witnessing a beating, and hesitates to send aid to the destitute.
Sitaram helps Udayaditya escape prison during a fire, opening his cell and leading him out into the open—undoing the imprisonment caused by the forged treason petition.

First, he ties thick sheets together into a rope, fastens it to a roof pillar, and carries Ramchandra Ray down on his back toward the boat below. At the rope’s end, he grips it with his teeth and carefully lowers Ramchandra into the boat, then jumps down himself.

Later, after Vibha faints in the king’s palace, Rammohan lifts her and carries her outside, places her in a palanquin, and returns to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is dressed by the Mahishi in conspicuous finery: thick gold bangles, diamond bracelets, a large nose ring, and an elaborate coiffure. Her shy, barely contained joy makes the preparation feel festive.

In Chandradwip, she goes in the opposite direction: dressed as a common woman, she rejects a palanquin and says she will go like a subject or beggar. She enters the palace like a maidservant, with no welcome; when her veil slips, she hastily pulls it back.

In his bedchamber, the window is bound to Surma’s absence: he leaves her place beside it empty and looks out at the familiar moonlight and garden, hoping she might still appear. In prison, the small window becomes a source of hope and inner freedom. The sky and birds remind him that his confinement may end; away from it, he feels surrounded by darkness and imprisoned even by the soft bed.

Sitaram first approaches Rukmini for money, mixing his requests with flirtatious banter and affectionate endearments, while she indulges him and lets him defer repayment. Their relationship turns covert as they scheme together, but when Udayaditya is imprisoned, Sitaram blames and threatens her, and she reveals how possessive she feels of the prince.

Later, after helping Udayaditya escape, Sitaram goes to Rukmini’s house intending to steal her money, assuming she is dead. He finds her alive, soaked and shaken after returning from the brink of death, and she vows to kill him and Udayaditya. Sitaram tries to soothe her with feigned affection; she grows more furious, goes for a blade, and he barely escapes. He then realizes she knows about the escape and flees Jessore with his family.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire as a distraction: it draws the guards away from Udayaditya’s door, letting him lead the prince out. He then turns the blaze into a cover-up. His men sabotage the firefighting, set fire to the now-empty prison cell, and plant bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword there. Staged shouts and Sitaram’s claim that the roof collapsed make the guards believe Udayaditya died in the fire; the burned sword and witnesses’ testimony help spread that story. Sitaram plans to use the supposed death to buy time, but when he learns Rukmini knows of the escape, he flees Jessore with his family.

In his court, Ramchandra joins in mocking Udayaditya, dismissing his rescue as something Udayaditya was simply expected to do—and believing he acted mainly to save his own sister, not out of concern for Ramchandra.

Pratapaditya dismisses the Emperor’s anger as “empty” and refuses to be deterred by the threat of Delhi’s soldiers. Later, Sitaram and Bhagavat exploit that very fear: they forge a petition, stamped with Udayaditya’s seal, claiming the prince is accusing his father of treason to win the kingdom. Bhagavat presents it to Pratapaditya as proof his son has appealed to the Emperor, turning the Delhi threat into a pretext to imprison Udayaditya.

When Surma is present, Vibha can slip away from her mother’s imposed grooming and have Surma arrange her hair as she likes—a quiet sign of their closeness and Surma’s care. After Surma is gone, Vibha waits for her to braid it, but evening comes and her hair remains unbraided. Later, it is described as unkempt, reflecting how Surma’s absence leaves Vibha lonely and uncared for.
